title: A Cray-1 supercomputer replica from 30 "obsolete" Mac Minis
gist: Spain's Museo de Historia de la Computación built a 1:1 visual replica of the 1976 Cray-1 powered by 30 2012-era Mac Minis, reaching 1.3 teraflops versus the original's roughly 160 megaflops. The fan-free build uses passive convection, and the team hopes to crowdfund 70-80 M4 Mac Minis to reach the TOP500.

insights.claim: The museum's 1:1 Cray-1 replica took 18 months and is a 50th-anniversary tribute to the Cray-1 and Apple's founding.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
entities: Museo de Historia de la Computación
insights.locator: The Museo de Historia de la Computación

insights.claim: Thirty mostly 2012 Mac Minis (five quad-core i7, 25 dual-core i5) deliver 1.3 teraflops across 64 active cores, down from a previous 1.5 teraflops on 70 cores before a node went offline, measured with a custom Python matrix-multiplication script.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Shows decade-old consumer hardware now far exceeds historic supercomputers.
insights.locator: Mac Minis from over a decade ago

insights.claim: The original Cray-1 peaked at about 160 megaflops using vector processing, whereas the replica distributes work across independent processors in a parallel cluster.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Illustrates the architectural shift from vector machines to commodity parallel clusters.
insights.locator: The replica is a valuable tool

insights.claim: Consumer hardware in the replica is vastly more capable than the purpose-built research machine that inspired it.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Illustrates how fast compute price-performance has fallen.
insights.quote: consumer hardware that’s vastly more capable than the machine that inspired it
insights.locator: The replica is a valuable tool

insights.claim: The team chose macOS Mojave (10.14) over a standard Linux distribution because of macOS's built-in Message Passing Interface support for passing tasks between nodes.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Practical detail on cluster orchestration with legacy software.
insights.locator: Rather than opting for a more standard Linux distribution

insights.claim: Mounting Mac Minis vertically in a steel chassis with aluminum trays makes the tower a thermal chimney, removing the need for fans and making the cluster nearly inaudible compared with data centers.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Passive convection is an alternative to loud fan cooling at small scale; not shown to scale to data centers.

insights.claim: The only notable noise comes from two gigabit Ethernet switches at 30-33 decibels, which the team plans to replace with silent models, while each Mac Mini produces 12-15 dBA at idle.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge

insights.claim: The control terminal blends DEC VT05 and Processor Technology Sol-20 designs with an analog control panel, uses one master Mac Mini to direct all nodes, and uses modern Samsung flat displays instead of CRTs to avoid connectivity headaches.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Design trade-off of authenticity versus practicality.

insights.claim: The team hopes to crowdfund 70-80 additional M4 Mac Minis to fill the tower's empty half and build a cluster capable of ranking on the TOP500 list.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Speculative goal with no funding secured; low-probability item.

insights.claim: The replica is on permanent display alongside two unused authentic Cray CX1 systems, with guided tours Saturdays from 11:30 am to 2 pm.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
entities: Museo de Historia de la Computación
insights.locator: The replica is on permanent display
